title: Soichiro Honda's Piston Rings and the Diploma He Never Collected
dek: In the late 1930s a Hamamatsu garage owner went back to class to learn about metal, skipped the exams, and then had to learn again when Toyota tested his rings.

story.event: Studying metallurgy part time after failed piston rings, then failing Toyota's inspection
story.summary: In the late 1930s Soichiro Honda, who ran a garage in Hamamatsu, set up Tokai Seiki to make piston rings; after repeated failures he studied metallurgy part time at the Hamamatsu Industrial Institute for nearly two years, without sitting the exams or taking a diploma. When production began, only three of fifty rings passed Toyota's quality inspection, and he spent nearly two more years studying manufacturing at universities and steelmakers before supplying Toyota and Nakajima Aircraft.
paragraphs: In 1936, by his company's own account, Soichiro Honda had a thriving garage in Hamamatsu, the local branch of the Tokyo repair firm Art Shokai, and had grown dissatisfied with repair work. He wanted to make something, and he chose piston rings. His investors refused: repairs were paying well, so why take the risk? He found another way, setting up a separate company, Tokai Seiki, with an acquaintance, Shichiro Kato, as its president. He worked at the garage by day and on the rings at night.

The rings kept failing. Honda later admitted that he had known nothing about the role of silicon: "we didn't even know we needed it." So, at about 31, the garage owner enrolled part time at the Hamamatsu Industrial Institute, today the engineering faculty of Shizuoka University, to study metallurgy. He carried what he heard in lectures back to his workshop. According to the AMA Motorcycle Hall of Fame, he did not sit the exams, and when told he would not graduate he said a diploma was "worth less than a movie theater ticket." Honda's company history says he worked and studied so hard for nearly two years that his face visibly changed.

By 1939 his trial rings worked. He handed the garage to his trainees, became president of Tokai Seiki and began production under a contract with Toyota. Then came the second lesson. Of fifty rings submitted for Toyota's quality inspection, only three met the standard. This time, his company's history says, the problem was not the metal but the manufacturing.

He did not retreat to repairs. For nearly two more years he visited universities and steelmakers across Japan to study how they made things, until Tokai Seiki could supply mass-produced rings to Toyota and to Nakajima Aircraft; at its height it employed more than 2,000 people. The war then took the company out of his hands. In 1942 Toyota took 40 per cent of it and Honda was moved down to senior managing director; bombing destroyed one plant and an earthquake in January 1945 brought down another. After Japan's surrender he sold out to Toyota, and in 1946 he started again with the Honda Technical Research Institute.

quote.text: Look not at the flask, but at what it contains: there may be a new flask full of old wine, and an old flask that has not even new wine in it
quote.source_title: Pirke Avot: The Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, tr. Joseph I. Gorfinkle, Project Gutenberg eBook #8547
quote.connection: Honda treated the diploma as a flask and cared only for what it held. Toyota's inspectors took the same view of his rings and found three good ones in fifty. Rabbi Meir's test frees you from the certificate, and it also leaves nothing but the contents to be judged.

reflection: Your profession leans on papers: qualifications, accreditation, signed results. Honda's story does not say they are worthless. It says they are containers, and that sooner or later someone tests what is inside, usually someone less patient than an examiner.

It also says that learning tends to come in rounds. Honda studied for two years to understand the metal, then needed nearly two more to learn how to make it the same way every time. If you are in a second round of learning something you thought you had already mastered, the first round was not wasted. That is often simply how the work goes.
invitation: Pick one task you understand in principle but have not yet done reliably. Do it once today, slowly, and write down the single step that came out differently from last time. That is enough for today.

research_notes: Order of events: the slate put the Toyota rejection before the schooling, as some popular accounts do. Honda's own heritage page and Cycle World (1997) both place the part-time study first (after early technical failures), then the start of production and the failed Toyota inspection, then nearly two more years of visits to universities and steelmakers; the story follows that order. Founding date: Honda's heritage page and ASME put the setting-up of Tokai Seiki in 1936; the AMA Hall of Fame (and Wikipedia) say 1937; Honda's Power Products page says he became president in 1936, while the heritage page and Tokyo Journal say he became president in 1939. The story uses 1936 for the setting-up, attributed to the company's account, and 1939 for the presidency. approx_date is 1937, when Honda (born 17 November 1906) turned 31 and, by the heritage page's 'nearly two years' before 1939, was studying. Outcome numbers: Honda's heritage page and Cycle World agree that three of fifty rings passed; Toyota's GAZOO site gives the same result as 47 of 50 returned as defective. The size of the Toyota order differs (Cycle World 50,000; GAZOO 30,000), so the story gives no order size. GAZOO also says stable production came two years later and that Honda obtained 28 patents; the patent count is not used. School name: Honda calls it the Hamamatsu Industrial Institute; other sources say Hamamatsu College of Technology or a technical high school (its formal name was the Hamamatsu Higher Technical School); all agree it is now Shizuoka University's engineering faculty, and the story uses Honda's name for it. The exam and diploma remark rests on the AMA Motorcycle Hall of Fame biography and is attributed to it; iN Hamamatsu independently describes him as auditing classes. The 1936 racing crash is left out because sources disagree on how badly Honda was hurt (Honda's heritage page says not seriously; Cycle World says it nearly killed him). Wikipedia's figure of 450,000 yen for the post-war sale (also given by GAZOO) is not used. Funding: the slate said bootstrapped; GAZOO says the venture used up most of the garage's earnings, but Honda's page says his investors refused and he set up the company with an acquaintance, Shichiro Kato, as president, and Toyota took 40% in 1942, so funding is given as mixed. GAZOO is in Japanese and does not spell Honda's name in Latin script, so the source checker cannot match it by name. Quote: Gorfinkle's note says some texts attribute this saying to 'Rabbi' (Judah ha-Nasi) rather than Rabbi Meir; the thinker follows Gorfinkle's main text.
